newsitem.title: USA: Orange County, Calif., launches Wall Street tour.
newsitem.headline: Orange County, Calif., launches Wall Street tour.

text.p: Top Orange County, Calif., officials met Thursday with Wall Street bankers and credit analysts hoping to boost confidence in the county a year after it emerged from bankruptcy.
Since emerging from bankruptcy last June, the county has sought to mend relations with bankers and investors still fuming over its 18-month-long financial crisis.

This week, the county stepped up its public relations effort, dispatching a team of senior officials to New York as part of a so-called investor "road show." In addition to New York, the officials were scheduled to hold events in Boston, Chicago and San Francisco.
Orange County shocked Wall Street in December 1994 when it filed for bankruptcy after losing more than $1.6 billion on risky investments made by its once respected treasurer, Robert Citron.

"We have a budget that makes sense, that balances the demands of our 2.6 million citizens. We have done significant restructuring in the last year," county Board of Supervisors Chairman William Steiner said in an interview.

The county's chief executive officer, Jan Mittermeier, said her $3.7 billion spending plan for fiscal year 1997-1998 would fund a reserve for emergencies of about $15 million, up from just $3 million. She said the county hoped this year to boost the reserve to $20 million.
The county's new "Credit and Debt Management" plan calls for it to build up a $140 million fund by fiscal year 2001-2002 to retire outstanding debt, officials said.

Christopher Varelas, a Salomon Bros. vice president and the county's senior financial advisor, said the efforts would improve the county's image on Wall Street and could lead to credit rating upgrades.
"The perception is going to improve," he said. "We realise it's going to take time."
